title: Chunked Output Graceful Drain Spec
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a pragmatic, kernel-friendly approach for delivering chunked/partial token outputs while preserving strong user-facing correctness guarantees and minimizing wasted compute on cancelled requests. The core idea is a two-tier graceful drain mechanism: emission fences at the scheduler/kernel boundary, and a higher-level graceful-drain policy that coordinates KV-cache commits, kernel preemption points, and client-visible flushes.

Context / motivation
- Current streaming behavior is: best-effort token emission from the runtime whenever the decoder produces bytes. Cancellation from the client or preemption for higher-priority requests often leads to: wasted last-microbatch compute, inconsistent partial tokens across retries, and KV-cache state that is half-applied.
- We need a solution that reduces both wasted GPU cycles and user-visible artifacts (e.g., truncated JSON objects mid-token, repeated partial prefixes).
- Constraints: must work with continuous batching, quantized models, and minimal scheduler changes to preserve throughput.

Goals
- Minimize wasted GPU work on cancel/preempt events (objective: reduce wasted token compute by >= 40% in p95 cancellation scenarios).
- Ensure partial-token emissions are reconstructable and consistent across retries (deterministic prefix semantics).
- Avoid complex cross-node coordination for KV-cache commits where possible; prefer local, best-effort guarantees with compensating telemetry and easy recovery modes.
- Be implementable with incremental changes to kernel scheduling and the serving runtime (no full rewrite).

Non-goals
- Strong multi-request transactional semantics for KV cache across nodes (out of scope).
- End-to-end strong consistency for partial outputs under all failure modes (we provide pragmatic heuristics and fallbacks).

Key concepts / vocabulary
- Emission fence: a lightweight, kernel-level marker associated with a microbatch boundary. A fence indicates that all output up to that point is logically flushable; preemption before a fence implies nothing has been emitted for the client.
- Graceful drain window: a short, configurable time window or token-count window after a cancel/preempt during which the runtime will allow in-flight microbatches to finish up to a fence and perform a coordinated flush/commit step.
- Partial-token reconciliation record (PTR): a compact record saved to local storage/trace containing the last emitted token boundary, KV cache snapshot pointer, and sequence id. Used to reconcile client retries and avoid duplicate/reformatted partial prefixes.
- Kernel preemption point: a place inside the kernel execution (e.g., after attention + MLP block) where the kernel can yield control with bounded work loss.

Design overview
1) Emission fences and microbatch boundaries
- Each microbatch execution annotates a fence ID and returns: emitted-bytes-since-fence and an internal fence-stable flag. The fence is created at a natural kernel boundary (end of a decode iteration or after KV-update).
- The kernel guarantees that if it hits a preemption before completing the fence, no emission corresponding to that fence will be handed to the network stack. That avoids partial-byte emission.

2) Graceful drain window policy
- On client cancel or server-initiated preempt, the scheduler starts a grace timer (default 20–50ms or configurable N tokens) per-request.
- If running microbatches can reach a fence within the window, they are allowed to complete and the emitter will send one final flush containing an ordered list of fence-complete outputs.
- If the fence cannot be reached within the grace window, the kernel is preempted and the latest fully-complete fence (if any) is flushed; otherwise nothing is emitted.

3) PTRs and partial-token semantics
- Before any fence-complete flush, the runtime writes a PTR in-memory (evictable) and to an optional local write-ahead log (WAL) when running in Dedicated/Private mode where durability is required. PTR fields: fence_id, last_complete_token_index, kv_cache_version, model_version, and epoch monotonic counter.
- Clients receive fence IDs with every flush. On reconnect/retry, the router can reconcile by asking for the last fence known to the client and resuming from the next token index. This avoids emitting duplicate prefixes.

4) KV-cache commit semantics
- KV-cache updates are logically tied to fence completions. The runtime only marks a local KV-cache delta as committed when its associated fence completes and the PTR is recorded.
- For multi-GPU sharded KV-cache, we maintain per-shard fence consensus via a tiny O(1) atomic bit in shared metadata (fast path) or fall back to a coordinator for rare edge cases. We expect the fast path to suffice for most workloads.

5) Kernel cooperativity and preemption points
- Kernels must expose inexpensive preemption checks at designated preemption points. At a preemption point, a kernel can either: finish to the next fence, or yield immediately. The scheduler uses a cost model to choose whether to allow completion based on grace window, request priority, and expected remaining kernel time.
- We recommend initially adding a preemption check at the end of the attention+kv-update stage (cheap to implement for most ops).

6) Emission formatting and JSON/markup safety
- To avoid mid-JSON object truncation, the emitter will post-process fence-complete outputs to ensure they end on safe boundaries where possible: whitespace boundaries, token boundaries that map to UTF-8 code point boundaries, and (for structured-mode) syntactic boundaries when the model emits structured tokens. If a fence ends mid-structure, add a short sentinel marker and emit the PTR; clients can decide how to render.
- Backwards compatibility: streaming clients that don't understand PT R/fences will still receive raw bytes, but will see fewer mid-token breakages because fences reduce mid-byte emission.

Operational tradeoffs
- Longer grace windows reduce wasted rerun work and make outputs more natural for clients, but increase tail latency for high-priority interrupts. Default 30ms is a starting point; we'll tune via experiments.
- Recording PTRs to durable WAL adds IO overhead. Recommend durable PTRs only for Dedicated/Private deployments with strict SLAs; hosted service uses in-memory PTR + telemetry and optional async persistence.
- Per-shard fence consensus requires small metadata ops during microbatch commit; cost negligible compared to decode compute but must be optimized (cache-line friendly).

Failure modes and recovery
- Node crash after flush but before PTR persisted: clients may observe emitted bytes that the system cannot resume from; fallback behavior: router will fall back to re-run from last durable checkpoint (coarser-grained), and UI will show a warning about possible duplicated prefix.
- Repeated rapid cancels: apply exponential backoff on grace window and track abuse metrics; consider dropping to immediate preempt if repeated within short windows to protect cluster throughput.

API/contract changes
- Slightly extended streaming envelope: include fence_id and model_version metadata JSON with each flush chunk. Example: {"fence_id":"f-1234","model_version":"v1.2","chunk":"..."}
- Reconnect flow: client may supply last_seen_fence_id; router will request PTR for that fence and resume from next token index. If unknown, resume conservative re-run from checkpoint.

Implementation plan (phased)
Phase 0 (experiment / kernel probes) - 2 weeks
- Add lightweight fence metadata in kernel-microbatch return structs. No scheduling changes; just emit fence IDs to logs and metrics.
- Instrument preemption point timings.
Phase 1 (scheduling + in-memory PTRs) - 4 weeks
- Scheduler: implement grace window logic and decision model for letting microbatches finish to fence.
- Emission layer: attach fence metadata to flushes and store in-memory PTRs.
- KV cache: mark local deltas tied to fence completion.
Phase 2 (durable PTRs + per-shard quick consensus) - 4 weeks
- WAL for PTRs in Dedicated; per-shard fence bits implemented with cache-line-friendly metadata updates.
- Add small RPC for per-shard fence queries (fast path atomic test-and-set).
Phase 3 (client rollouts and compatibility) - 2 weeks
- Add fence metadata to streaming protocol; update SDKs to optionally supply last_seen_fence_id during reconnects.
- Monitor telemetry and rollout.

Metrics / success criteria
- Wasted compute on cancellations (token-time lost) p95 reduced by >=40% vs baseline.
- Frequency of mid-JSON object truncations down by 80% in streaming logs.
- PTR write latency overhead (durable mode) < 0.5ms p95.
- No >2% regression in overall throughput in hosted mode at default grace window.

Testing plan
- Unit tests: kernel fence metadata roundtrip, PTR creation and in-memory lookup.
- Integration tests: simulated cancel at multiple points; verify flush/no-flush semantics and KV-cache consistency locally.
- Chaos test: node crash after flush but before PTR persistence; verify router fallback path.
- Performance: end-to-end load test with synthetic streams including high cancel rates.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve
- Exact default grace window: should it be time-based or token-count-based? (Hybrid feels best: 30ms OR 2 tokens.)
- Per-shard fence fast path: do we use a tiny atomic ring vs a centralized coordinator? Preference: atomic metadata in shared memory on same node for sharded-local, coordinator only when cross-node needed.
- PTR durability policy: which classes of customers require WAL by default? Proposal: Dedicated/Private YES, Hosted OPT-IN per model.

Docs / rollout notes for SDK/clients
- SDKs: expose "resume_from_fence(fence_id)" helper that will call the router to reconcile and resume. Provide examples in JS/Python.
- Backwards compatibility: servers can omit fence metadata; clients should cope by replacing missing fields with null and resuming coarsely.

Appendix: sample timeline for a single request that is cancelled mid-decode
1. Request A starts; kernel begins microbatch M1 and creates fence f1 at token index 10.
2. Kernel completes M1 and marks fence f1 complete; PTR written in-memory; emitter sends chunk with f1.
3. Client cancels just after M1; scheduler starts grace window (30ms). Kernel M2 is already queued and would reach fence f2 in ~12ms. Scheduler decides to let M2 finish into f2 and flush; PTR for f2 is recorded and flush sent.
4. Router receives cancel + subsequent reconnect; client resumes with last_seen_fence=f2 and server resumes from token index after f2.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally pragmatic: avoid heavy distributed transactions. The emphasis is on deterministic, observable fences and durable or best-effort PTRs depending on deployment tier.
- Request feedback especially on: fence placement (which kernel boundary is safest), default grace window values, and KV-cache per-shard fast-path design.
